title: DeepImageSearch: Benchmarking Multimodal Agents for Context-Aware Image Retrieval in Visual Histories
one_liner: Turn image retrieval into a multi-step search problem where the agent must navigate a sequence of past visuals to recover context that one image alone does not contain.
lead: Standard image retrieval often assumes that one query can be matched to one image in isolation. This paper studies a harder setting where the needed clue is spread across a visual history. The agent has to explore, remember earlier findings, and decide which views to inspect next. DeepImageSearch builds a benchmark for that setting and tests whether multimodal agents can retrieve the right target when context is distributed across time and place.

problem.h2: Why isolated image matching breaks on context-dependent search
paras: Some retrieval tasks cannot be solved by looking at one picture and one query alone. The needed clue may depend on what happened earlier in the stream, what was nearby in another view, or how several scenes relate to each other.

When context is distributed across a history, retrieval becomes a search problem. The agent must decide where to look next, what to remember from earlier views, and when it has gathered enough evidence to name the target.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Benchmark retrieval as autonomous exploration over visual histories so that agents are tested on whether they can gather and use distributed context.

panels.title: 1. A context-heavy query arrives
panels.viz_args: The query refers to clues spread across several earlier visuals
panels.caption: No single frame contains the whole answer.

panels.title: 2. A static retriever looks once
panels.viz_args: Direct matching checks isolated items and misses the history
panels.caption: That approach is weak because the clue depends on sequence context.

panels.title: 3. The agent explores the history
panels.caption: The agent moves through the history, keeps useful findings, and narrows the target.

panels.title: 4. Tools and memory support long searches
panels.viz_args: Fine-grained tools plus short-term and long-term memory guide navigation
panels.caption: The system can revisit useful evidence because it stores what matters from previous steps.

panels.title: 5. Context-aware retrieval succeeds
panels.caption: The target is found because the agent assembled clues from multiple points in the visual history.

steps.text: Create retrieval tasks where the answer depends on relationships spread across connected visual histories.
Use a human-model pipeline to discover candidate clues across sequences so that benchmark creation can scale.
Let the system inspect views, move through the history, and store findings because one fixed snapshot is not enough.
Keep local recent details and broader past findings so that long searches do not lose earlier evidence.
Evaluate whether the agent can recover the right target when success requires multi-step context gathering.

paras: The paper changes the retrieval unit from a single query-image pair to a search process over a connected visual history. It asks whether the agent can recover context before it decides what to retrieve.
object.object: the retrieval policy that chooses where to inspect next and what evidence to keep

hidden.name: where the decisive context is located in the visual history
paras: The key hidden quantity is the location of the useful context. The agent knows the query, but it does not know which part of the visual history contains the clue that resolves it.

That hidden location can span several positions. One view might reveal a place, another might reveal an object, and a later one might connect them. The agent needs memory and search because the answer emerges only after these clues are combined.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark positions or relations in the history where the decisive context is most likely to be hiding.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is where the missing clue lives in the sequence of visuals.
The benchmark matters because it forces the agent to search for that clue instead of assuming each image can be judged alone.

mechanism.h2: Why this works: convert retrieval into guided exploration
paras: A plain retriever fails here because it scores isolated similarity. When the clue is distributed across several views, isolated scoring misses the relation that actually answers the query.

DeepImageSearch addresses this by giving the agent search actions and memory. The agent can inspect one part of the history, store a clue, move elsewhere, and combine the evidence later. This works because the retrieval decision is postponed until enough context has been gathered.

stages.s: Context-dependent query plus a connected visual history
Navigate the history with retrieval tools
Store and combine clues across steps
Choose the target after enough context is assembled because the history now supports the decision
A retrieval answer that depends on explored context rather than one isolated match

math.h2: Score a search path by clue gathering and final retrieval
math.words: A simple summary is to score each search path by how well it gathers useful context and whether the final retrieved item is correct. Paths with both properties should rank higher.
symbols: overall value of one exploration path through the visual history
quality of the final retrieved target
usefulness of the clues gathered during navigation

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Path A jumps to a target after one view.
Its retrieval value is 4 and its context value is 0, so with delta equal to 1 its total score is 4.
Path B inspects three linked views, stores a clue, and then chooses the target.
Its retrieval value is 4 and its context value is 3, so the total score is 7.
The later path is better because it collected the missing context before deciding.

math.note: The paper uses a fuller framework, but this score captures the reason an agentic approach can help when context lives across a history.

charts.title: Static multimodal retrieval baselines
charts.note: Strong single-step retrieval systems struggle because they are not built to search through distributed context.

charts.title: Agentic retrieval baseline with tools and memory
charts.note: The agentic setup performs better because it can inspect, remember, and combine evidence before making the retrieval decision.

items.b: Search can wander through irrelevant parts of the history.
items.html: If the navigation policy is weak, the agent may spend many steps chasing unhelpful clues because the correct branch was not recognized early.

items.b: Memory summaries can discard the deciding detail.
items.html: A stored summary may keep the broad story while dropping the exact clue needed later, so the final decision still fails.

items.b: Benchmark queries may favor certain clue patterns.
items.html: If query construction repeats similar forms, agents can learn those patterns too closely because they see the same style of distributed clue again and again.
The benchmark is useful because it tests whether retrieval systems can search for context rather than only score isolated similarity.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small connected photo history, such as a walk through a building with several rooms. Ask queries whose answer depends on combining clues from more than one image, such as identifying an item that was seen near one object and later moved to another place.

Compare a direct image matcher against an agent that can browse the history and keep notes. The demo should show that the browsing agent wins because it can collect clues across multiple views before naming the target.
demo.metric_eq: context_gain = accuracy_agentic - accuracy_static ; clue_use_rate = used_saved_clues / total_queries
demo.closing: The point is to show that context-aware retrieval is a search problem when the answer is distributed across a visual history.
